title: Seawater magnetohydrodynamic propulsion at propeller-class efficiency

concept.text: The innovation would make seawater magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) propulsion a practical, efficient way to propel ships. In a conduction MHD thruster, electric current passes through seawater inside a magnetic field. Their interaction produces a Lorentz force that pushes the water and generates thrust without a rotating propeller. The propulsion principle has already been demonstrated; the proposed breakthrough is achieving useful ship-scale performance with equipment that a vessel can carry, power and maintain.

Proposed performance scope: a seagoing thruster would convert 55–70% of its total electrical input into useful propulsive power at a declared service speed, including electrode power, cryogenic equipment and other propulsion auxiliaries. This numerical range preserves the candidate's ambition, but it is a proposed target. The supplied evidence does not verify its original attribution as a conventional propeller open-water efficiency benchmark, and that component-level measure would not by itself provide a like-for-like comparison with total electrical-to-propulsive efficiency.

significance.text: Efficient, maintainable MHD propulsion would turn a demonstrated electromagnetic propulsion principle into a potentially important marine engineering capability. Removing the propeller and its shaft would eliminate the thrust-producing device's blade-related noise and blade cavitation. It could also remove associated blade erosion and some drivetrain components. Those direct changes would give naval architects a different set of propulsion design options.

Propeller removal does not establish complete vessel silence or overall mechanical simplicity. Water flow, electrical equipment and cryogenic machinery remain relevant, and the Yamato-1 report explicitly describes onboard refrigerators for reliquefying helium. Acoustic performance, maintenance burden and overall reliability would therefore need separate measurements rather than being inferred from the absence of rotating blades.

Conditional synthesis: if the efficiency, equipment mass, reliability and acoustic advantages proved competitive, MHD propulsion could support quieter vessels and different arrangements of propulsion equipment. The research's transistor analogy expresses a judgment about the significance of a device-level change; it is not a source-backed prediction of comparable economic impact. Electromagnetic thrust would still have to overcome hull friction and wave drag, and would not itself create a supercavitating operating regime or remove displacement-hull speed constraints.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central physical barrier is seawater's low electrical conductivity, which creates substantial Joule dissipation when current is driven through it. Delannoy, Montero, Zapata and Machicoane's 2025 analysis separates channel electrical input into Joule losses and mechanical power, while also treating electrode and hydraulic losses. This supports a serious efficiency problem, but not the universal assertion that most total electrical input becomes heat at every operating point.

The missing engineering capability is an integrated propulsion system that combines strong magnetic fields, suitable channel dimensions and controlled hydraulic losses with manageable electrode and cryogenic requirements. Stronger fields and larger interaction lengths improve the modeled prospects, but a favorable channel calculation does not establish a favorable shipboard system once auxiliary electricity, equipment mass and operating requirements are included. The documented use of superconducting magnets and helium refrigeration illustrates the integration burden.

Proposed practical scope: the system must deliver sustained net thrust with magnets, electrodes, cooling and power equipment that remain maintainable aboard a working vessel. Conductivity enhancement, including the research's suggestion of wake doping, remains a possible approach rather than an established prerequisite. The supplied evidence likewise does not establish fields of tens of tesla or megawatt power as mandatory completion conditions. Such choices would need justification for a particular vessel and operating mission.

current_state.text: The supplied report by Sasakawa, Takezawa, Sugawara and Kyotani describes Yamato-1 as a 30 m, 185 tonne experimental vessel whose sea-running tests began on 16 June 1992. Its readable prose reports speed trials up to 2 T and a speed of 5.3 knots at 2 T. Approximately 7.5 knots at 4 T was an extrapolation, not a reported measured result. The report concluded that the system could not then compete in propulsion efficiency with conventional propulsion, but the supplied review identifies no numerical Yamato-1 efficiency that would justify calling it a measured few-percent result.

The Yamato-1 evidence has important extraction limits: the reviewed archive OCR contains missing pages and damaged tables despite being presented as full text. The dimensions and trial results above are supported by the readable material identified in the review. The candidate's attribution to proceedings published on 1 April 1995 was not established internally by that material and is therefore not treated as verified publication metadata.

Delannoy et al. (2025), DOI 10.22364/mhd.61.1-2.6, summarize Yamato as a 30 m boat reaching 5.5 knots with 4 T superconducting magnets. That condensed description does not distinguish magnet capability from the operating field during the reported speed trial. It should therefore remain separate from the earlier report's more specific distinction between measured performance at 2 T and extrapolation to 4 T; the supplied evidence does not resolve the descriptions into a demonstrated 4 T speed trial.

Delannoy et al.'s scale-up calculation uses a 10 T field and a 5 m interaction length and gives a vessel speed of 3 m/s with 8.8% boat or thruster efficiency and 17% pump efficiency under unchanged loss and drag parameters. A further modeled case reaches 20% after assumed reductions in those parameters. These are calculations, not full-scale trials. Their efficiency accounting uses channel power and does not demonstrate the proposed total-system efficiency with cryogenic auxiliaries included. The supplied review describes a complete text extraction of the paper, but its figure images were not inspected.

The research also reports a December 2024 miniature high-temperature-superconductor MHD boat reaching 4.0 cm/s, or 41.7% of its calculated speed, and describes a full-size extension as a design calculation. These details remain unverified within the supplied evidence because no saved text from the cited TRID record was available to the review. Their absence from the captured evidence does not show that the reported result is false, but it prevents treating the numbers, publication details or scale-up description as confirmed achievements here.

Neither of the two reviewed source artifacts demonstrates seawater MHD propulsion near 90% efficiency or at the proposed 55–70% total-system target. The historical trial and the 2025 calculations establish dated achievements and limitations. They do not establish a field-wide absence of subsequent advances: the supplied freshness record contains no bounded search evidence supporting a comprehensive assessment as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: a crewed or large unmanned vessel would sustain a declared service speed of several knots for hours using seawater MHD thrust as its sole source of propulsion, while achieving measured total electrical-to-useful-propulsive-power efficiency of 55–70%. These duration, speed and efficiency thresholds are proposed criteria for this record, not established standards or demonstrated feasibility limits.
completion_criteria.label: Sole-MHD propulsion sustains hours at several knots with 55–70% efficiency

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement boundary: define useful propulsive power as net installed thruster thrust multiplied by vessel speed. Count electrode electricity, cryogenic electricity and other propulsion auxiliaries in the input, and account for changes in stored electrical, magnetic or thermal energy so that precharged or precooled equipment cannot conceal part of the operating cost. Report channel, pump and whole-system efficiencies separately, together with measurement uncertainty and the method used to determine net thrust. Any comparison with conventional propulsion should use explicitly matched energy boundaries and operating conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Report whole-system efficiency with full energy accounting and measurement uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: repeated trials, preferably with independent measurement or replication, should document vessel size and load, speed, seawater conditions, magnetic field, equipment mass, auxiliary demand and maintenance needs. Endurance and acoustic claims should receive their own measurements. A centimetres-per-second tank model, static mooring pull or calculated scale-up would demonstrate narrower capabilities and would not satisfy the proposed seagoing scope. Successful finite trials would establish performance over the tested operating envelope, not universal efficiency across all vessels and sea conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated seagoing trials document operating conditions and practical performance limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MNE-01, Ship-scale collapse of turbulent skin friction, and MNE-02, Merchant ships freed from the displacement-hull speed barrier, address resistance and operating-speed constraints. MNE-03 addresses the production of thrust. A vessel might combine advances in those areas, but efficient electromagnetic propulsion alone would not demonstrate either reduction in turbulent skin friction or escape from displacement-hull constraints.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-04, Controlled, sustained supercavitating travel, concerns maintaining a distinct cavity-based travel regime. Eliminating propeller-blade cavitation through MHD propulsion is a different capability from sustaining a cavity around a vehicle. Neither achievement entails the other, so the concepts remain separate.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-05, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing; MNE-06, Through-seawater links beyond the acoustic range–rate ceiling; and MNE-10, Coherent observability of the deep-ocean volume, concern positioning, communications and observation. A quieter propulsion system could conditionally benefit some sensing missions, but it would not itself solve any of those capabilities. The supplied titles support these broad distinctions, not a detailed technical assessment of overlap.

Roster-based synthesis: MNE-07, Persistent abyssal work, with depth no longer the cost driver, could depend on propulsion among many other systems. MNE-08, Work-class underwater vehicles powered by the ocean, concerns energy supply, whereas MHD propulsion consumes supplied electrical energy to create thrust. MNE-09, Storm-stable floating land in the open ocean, concerns stability and habitability rather than propulsion efficiency. Possible integration does not justify merging these entries.

The research's statement that this concept also covers historical items 2 and 6 cannot be assessed because those historical descriptions were not supplied. Their numbering should not be assumed to identify MNE-02 and MNE-06 in the present roster. Routine improvements to bladed propulsors remain outside MNE-03's central scope, which is practical seawater electromagnetic thrust.

change_log.change: Preserved MNE-03's identity while describing the breakthrough as practical, efficient realization of an already demonstrated propulsion principle.
change_log.reason: Yamato-1 establishes historical seawater MHD propulsion; the missing capability concerns useful integrated performance.

change_log.change: Retained 55–70% as a proposed total-system target and removed its treatment as a verified conventional benchmark.
change_log.reason: No saved source text verifies the original open-water efficiency attribution, and conventional component efficiency differs from total electrical-to-propulsive efficiency.

change_log.change: Replaced the universal majority-of-input heat-loss claim with substantial conductivity-related Joule losses.
change_log.reason: The reviewed equations establish the loss mechanism without establishing that fraction at every operating point.

change_log.change: Separated blade-related acoustic and cavitation benefits from claims of complete silence and overall simplicity.
change_log.reason: Cryogenic machinery, power equipment and water flow remain, and whole-vessel acoustic performance was not demonstrated.

change_log.change: Preserved Yamato-1's measured 5.3 knots at 2 T, separated the 7.5-knot extrapolation at 4 T and retained the differing 2025 summary with its ambiguity.
change_log.reason: The earlier report distinguishes measurement from extrapolation more specifically than the later summary.

change_log.change: Added the modeled 20% improved-loss case and the 17% pump figure alongside the 8.8% case, with explicit channel-power boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original text omitted useful modeled detail and could be read as reporting comprehensive shipboard efficiency.

change_log.change: Retained the miniature HTS boat's reported quantitative results with an explicit evidence limitation.
change_log.reason: Missing saved TRID text prevents verification but does not establish that the report is false.

change_log.change: Removed unsupported mandatory requirements for wake doping, tens-of-tesla fields and megawatt power.
change_log.reason: The evidence supports scaling dependencies without establishing those particular implementation choices as necessary.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion accounting, reproducibility and operating-envelope requirements.
change_log.reason: Auxiliary demand, stored-energy changes and mismatched efficiency denominators could otherwise obscure whether the intended capability had been demonstrated.

change_log.change: Replaced the asserted historical overlap with explicit distinctions across the supplied concept roster.
change_log.reason: The roster provides relevant neighboring concepts, while historical items 2 and 6 lack supplied descriptions.

change_log.change: Qualified present-day conclusions and retained source extraction limits.
change_log.reason: Dated artifacts and an empty freshness record cannot establish the entire field's status in November 2026; partial OCR also limits historical interpretation.

unresolved_issues: The conventional open-water efficiency range and two-thirds power-conversion attribution remain unverified because no saved text from the cited ScienceDirect material was supplied.
The relationship between Yamato-1's reported 2 T speed trials and the later 5.5-knot summary mentioning 4 T magnets remains unresolved.
The supplied review does not establish the Yamato-1 report's claimed publication date or proceedings attribution.

The reported miniature HTS boat results—4.0 cm/s and 41.7% of calculated speed—and its publication and scale-up details require source verification. They are retained as qualified reports rather than deleted as the review's proposed replacement suggested, because missing evidence does not disprove them.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether later work has achieved materially higher total-system efficiency or changed the practical gap as of November 2026.
The feasibility of the proposed 55–70% total-system target, and the equipment and operating conditions required to reach it, remain unestablished.
Historical items 2 and 6 cannot be reconciled with this concept without their original descriptions.

brief.title: Efficient ship propulsion without propellers
possible: Ships could travel without a rotating propeller while turning more than half their propulsion electricity into useful motion. Electric current passing through seawater inside a magnetic field would push the water, producing thrust.
The goal is a seagoing system whose magnets, cooling equipment and power supplies a working vessel could carry and maintain.
why: Removing propeller blades would remove their noise and the damage caused by bubbles forming and collapsing around them. Ship designers would gain different ways to arrange propulsion equipment, with fewer associated drivetrain parts.

sources.who: Y. Delannoy, I. Montero, A. Zapata and N. Machicoane
sources.showed: They tested a seawater pump and a model boat driven by electricity and magnets. Their calculations reached 20% boat efficiency after assuming reduced losses and drag.
sources.quote:
Results at higher voltages are
disturbed by the presence of gas in the channel due to electrolysis at the electrodes.
sources.cited_for: Their experiments and calculations explain the energy losses and the demands of scaling up.
sources.not_established: The calculations do not demonstrate an efficient seagoing system with cooling and other equipment included.

sources.who: Yohei Sasakawa, Setsuo Takezawa, Yoshinori Sugawara and Yoshihiro Kyotani
sources.showed: Their experimental vessel, Yamato-1, reached 5.3 knots using electromagnetic propulsion. Its propulsion efficiency could not compete with conventional systems.
sources.quote:
Refrigerators to reliquefy helium evaporated on account of heat 
intrusion are mounted on board, whilst a large-sized cooling 
equipment for initial cooling of superconducting coils is 
installed on shore to reduce the ship weight and to make the 
thrusters compact.
sources.cited_for: A vessel demonstrated the propulsion principle at sea and exposed the burden of cooling its magnets.
sources.not_established: The trials did not demonstrate competitive propulsion efficiency.

sources.who: Researchers behind the miniature boat study
sources.showed: This is an experimental study of a miniature boat using magnets that require cooling, with a calculated design for a full-size version.
sources.cited_for: The study concerns another small-scale demonstration of electromagnetic propulsion.
sources.not_established: A miniature boat experiment and a calculated larger design do not establish practical seagoing performance.

shown: Yamato-1 demonstrated that electricity and magnets could propel a vessel at sea, reaching 5.3 knots. It established that the principle works, but its efficiency could not compete with conventional propulsion.

Delannoy and colleagues tested a pump and a small boat, then calculated larger designs. One modeled case reached 20% boat efficiency after assumed improvements. It did not include all the electricity a shipboard system would need.
missing: A seagoing vessel has yet to demonstrate the proposed efficiency while relying entirely on electromagnetic thrust.
The full electricity cost must include cooling, power supplies and changes in energy stored before a trial.
Magnets, electrodes and cooling equipment must work together with manageable weight, energy losses and maintenance.
Repeated sea trials must establish endurance, noise and reliability under documented operating conditions.

milestones.label: Sustained sea travel at the proposed efficiency
milestones.explanation: A crewed or large unmanned vessel would have to sustain several knots for hours using only electromagnetic thrust at the proposed efficiency target. This would establish useful propulsion beyond a model or brief trial.

milestones.label: Whole-system efficiency with complete energy accounting
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to relate net thrust and vessel speed to all propulsion electricity, including cooling and stored energy, with uncertainty reported. This would make efficiency claims meaningful and comparable.

milestones.label: Repeated sea trials establish practical performance limits
milestones.explanation: Repeated sea trials would have to document vessel load, seawater conditions, equipment demands and maintenance, with separate endurance and noise measurements. This would establish where the system performs reliably.

uncertain: Can strong enough magnets and sufficiently low losses deliver the proposed efficiency in equipment a working vessel can carry?
How much quieter and easier to maintain would the complete vessel be once water flow, electrical equipment and cooling machinery are included?
Which operating conditions and energy boundaries would make comparisons with conventional propulsion fair?
